title: I Locked My Manager Out of the Break Room He Weaponized

parts.text: I swiped my badge at 2:17 a.m. and the door chirped anyway. Derek had taped a yellow rule to the microwave: ten-minute breaks, no exceptions. I was thirty-one, night-shift supervisor, holding a mug that still smelled like burnt Folgers. "Ten minutes," Derek said, hovering in the doorway. "I timed you last Tuesday." I looked at the vending-machine clock. "You timed me while I reset a pallet jack." He shrugged. "Policy is policy." Someone had left a crushed chocolate-chip granola bar on the table. My crew watched through the glass. Derek loved that doorway. He loved the laminated AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL sign like it made him a cop. At 2:26 he clapped. "Back on the floor." My badge clip popped off and skittered under the fridge. "Safety violation," he said. "Write yourself up." I reached under the fridge and my fingers hit a spare master fob labeled in Sharpie: BREAK RM OVERRIDE. His handwriting. Same as the yellow rule. I closed my fist around it. Then the PA cracked on with his voice, even though he stood five feet away. "Break room is closed until further notice. Supervisor included." The magnetic lock clicked. I was still inside. Derek smiled through the glass, waiting to see if I would beg.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: He thinks the lock proves he owns the room; I still have his override fob and the radio is live.

social.video_title: He locked me in at 2 a.m. — Part 1/2
social.description: Night shift, a ten-minute rule, and a fridge that hid more than crumbs. I found his override fob while he watched through the glass. Would you have used it immediately?

parts.text: I pressed the fob to the reader and the lock thunked open like it had been waiting. Derek's smile dropped so fast his radio bumped the glass. "That's not yours," he said. I stepped out and held the fob toward the cameras. "It was under the fridge you made me crawl to." The burnt coffee almost smelled friendly. I printed my punches and circled every ten-minute break he had interrupted with a fourteen-minute safety talk. "You can't post that," Derek said. "Watch me," I said, and taped it beside his yellow rule. Marisol from packing stopped laughing when she saw the Sharpie label. "He's been closing this room during inspections so nobody sits," she said. I radioed facilities on the channel Derek still had live. "Need a lock change. Unofficial master on site." They answered in twelve seconds. Derek grabbed for the fob. I dropped it into the metal suggestion box with the slot nobody can fish. HR called at 6:40 a.m. while I ate a cold Egg McMuffin in my truck. They asked about mediation. I asked for the camera clip, the fob, and the yellow rule in my file. By noon Derek was realigned to inventory in a building without a door he could trap people behind. I kept my mug. The new sign says BREAKS ARE BREAKS.

social.video_title: I used his own fob on camera — Part 2/2
social.description: The lock clicked, the radio was still live, and facilities hates unofficial masters. The suggestion box did the rest. Was locking someone in a break room ever management?
